titre: Eijkman, Beriberi, and the Replaced Cook
accroche: In Batavia, chickens fed polished rice become paralyzed after a change of cook. Eijkman draws the cause of beriberi from it, but not the right explanation.
contenu_vulgarise:
In Batavia, in the Dutch East Indies, the laboratory directed by Christiaan Eijkman is housed temporarily in the military hospital; he will direct it from 1888 to 1896. Since 1886, a commission sent from Holland has been looking for the cause of beriberi, a disease that paralyzes, leaves its victims short of breath, and kills soldiers, sailors, and prisoners. It believed it had found a bacterium; the disinfection measures it recommended did not have the hoped-for success. Eijkman, who stayed on site, makes no more progress. Then the laboratory's chickens fall ill.

## A Henhouse Disease

The birds stagger, can no longer perch, collapse onto their sides; paralysis spreads to the respiratory muscles. Under the microscope, it is a polyneuritis, that is, damage to several nerves, as in the sick people. Eijkman looks for an infection: no microorganism, and all the chickens are affected, even those kept apart as controls. When the epidemic dies out, the investigation stops for lack of sick birds.

The lead comes next from the kitchen. To save money, the laboratory's keeper had been feeding the chickens cooked rice obtained from the hospital kitchens. The cook changes; his successor refuses to give military rice to civilian poultry. From June 17 to November 27, the chickens therefore eat polished rice. The disease breaks out on July 10 and dies out in the last days of November, after five months of polished rice.

## From Chicken to Prisoner

Eijkman puts the hypothesis to the test. Chickens fed cooked polished rice fall ill after three to four weeks; those that eat unpolished rice stay healthy, and many of the sick recover when their ration is changed. Sago and tapioca cause the same disease. The protective principle is found in the silver skin of the grain, its inner covering, along with the germ, and dissolves in water or alcohol. It is called bran when it is set aside in polishing.

The question remains whether humans are affected. At Eijkman's request, the medical inspector Vorderman investigates 101 prisons in Java, nearly 300,000 inmates. Where the rice served is polished, beriberi is about 300 times more frequent. The results are at first greeted with skepticism.

## The Cause, Without the Right Explanation

Eijkman rules out simple hunger, lack of protein, or lack of salts. But, as the Nobel Prize presentation speech recalls, one could easily imagine a poison. He makes it his working hypothesis: a poison would form, rendered harmless by the protective substance in the bran. His attempts to establish it remain in vain.

It is his successor in Java, Grijns, who shows that the substance is used directly by the body, and that the diet must contain, in addition to the known constituents, other substances necessary for health. The discovery does not bring an immediate decline in beriberi: people balk at replacing polished rice, doubt that the polyneuritis of birds is the same disease, and poorly appreciate Eijkman's work.

The 1929 Nobel Prize in Medicine goes to Eijkman and Frederick Hopkins. Grijns is not among them.

repere.texte: In the prisons where polished rice was served, beriberi was about 300 times more frequent than in those where unpolished rice was served (Vorderman's survey: 101 prisons, nearly 300,000 inmates).
repere.source: Christiaan Eijkman, Nobel lecture “Antineuritic Vitamin and Beriberi,” 1929 (retranslated from the French; original wording not retrieved)

carte.punch: A replaced cook, paralyzed chickens: the clue that led to the cause of beriberi.
carte.idee: In Batavia, laboratory chickens fed polished rice become paralyzed. Eijkman draws the cause of beriberi from it, but supposes a poison neutralized by bran. It is his successor Grijns who understands that it is a deficiency in the diet.

quiz.question: What mechanism did Eijkman suppose to explain the protective effect of rice bran?
choix: A bacterium that the bran destroyed
A lack of calories that the bran made up
A lack of protein that the bran supplied
A poison that a substance in the bran neutralized
quiz.explication: Eijkman made the poison his working hypothesis, without being able to establish it; the idea of a deficiency came from his successor Grijns. Infection had been sought and then ruled out: no microorganism was found. Simple hunger and lack of protein or salts, according to him, could not cause the disease either.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did the laboratory's chickens start eating polished rice?
choix: Military rice ran short in the hospital's stores
The new cook refused to give military rice to the poultry
Eijkman wanted to test the effect of polished rice on animals
The laboratory's keeper found polished rice cheaper
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The keeper fed the chickens with the cooked rice from the hospital kitchens; when the cook changed, his successor refused to give military rice to civilian poultry, and the chickens switched to polished rice.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Vorderman's survey in the prisons of Java show?
choix: Beriberi affected prisons serving polished rice as much as the others
Prisons serving unpolished rice had more cases of beriberi
Beriberi was about 300 times more frequent where the rice served was polished
Inmates fed polished rice recovered from beriberi faster
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Across 101 prisons and nearly 300,000 inmates, Vorderman found that beriberi was about 300 times more frequent where polished rice was served, which pointed toward diet rather than infection.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who showed that the protective substance in bran was a missing element in the diet, and not an antidote to a poison?
choix: Frederick Hopkins, who shares the Nobel Prize with Eijkman in 1929
The Pekelharing-Winkler commission, sent from Holland in 1886
Vorderman, the medical inspector who investigated the prisons of Java
Grijns, who succeeded Eijkman as head of the Java laboratory
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It was Grijns, Eijkman's successor in Java, who showed that the substance was used directly by the body: the diet had to contain substances other than those already known. Eijkman had been unable to establish his hypothesis of a poison.
